analysis.one_liner: Directs federal regulators to write rules against fraudulent telemarketing and lets states sue to enforce them.
analysis.headline: The bill passed both the Senate and House by voice vote with no recorded opposition, but the House never approved the Senate's final changes before the 102nd Congress ended, so it died without becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules against fraudulent and abusive telephone sales: requiring prompt shipping and refunds, letting buyers cancel orders, restricting the hours when sales calls can be made, and banning computer-generated calls that hang up on people. It let state attorneys general sue fraudulent telemarketers in federal court and created a federal clearinghouse where people could check out phone sellers. A Senate version became a House-passed version, but the two chambers never finished reconciling the text before Congress adjourned.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary phone consumers targeted by prize scams, boiler-room operators, and fraudulent sellers would gain federal protections: guaranteed shipping deadlines and refunds, cancellation rights, limits on when sales calls can come, and a government clearinghouse to check out sellers. State attorneys general would gain the power to sue fraudulent telemarketers in federal court on behalf of their residents, and the FTC would gain stronger enforcement tools, including criminal contempt authority for violators of its court orders.

how_it_helps.text: The FTC had to write rules within 180 days requiring goods sold by phone to be shipped within a set period or refunded, giving buyers a cancellation window, restricting the hours when unsolicited sales calls could be made, and prohibiting computer-generated calls that the person called cannot end.
The bill defined 'credit card laundering' — routing fraudulent phone-sale charges through third parties to payment networks — as a fraudulent telemarketing practice that the FTC must prohibit.
State attorneys general could bring federal court actions to enjoin fraudulent telemarketing patterns, enforce FTC rules, and obtain damages for their states' residents.

The FTC gained authority to bring criminal contempt actions against people who violate its court orders in false advertising cases, and its civil investigative demands were extended to physical evidence such as products and recordings.

The FTC was directed to set up a clearinghouse for inquiries to federal agencies about telemarketing, so consumers could check on sellers, and to study deceptive practices in the life care home industry.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing firms would bear compliance costs — shipping deadlines, mandatory refunds, calling-hour limits, recordkeeping, and a ban on abusive prerecorded calls — and fraudulent operators would lose the credit card laundering workaround. Banks and payment networks would bear modest administrative costs from the records-release provision.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action required over $50,000 in actual damages for each person harmed, which put most individual fraud victims outside the door; they would depend on the FTC and state attorneys general rather than being able to sue themselves.
The core provisions — the FTC rules, state actions, and private actions — were set to expire five years after enactment, so Congress would have to act again to keep them alive.

The bill amended the Right to Financial Privacy Act to let a bank delay notifying a customer that the customer's records were released to a government authority, if a court found notice would let the customer dissipate assets tied to fraud — a trade-off of customer privacy for asset protection.

Securities brokers, dealers, investment advisers, and commodity traders were carved out of the FTC's rules and left to the SEC and CFTC to regulate separately, so protection would vary by which agency covered the pitch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and widespread harm — telephone fraud — with relatively modest costs to legitimate marketers, who would face compliance chores but keep operating; the biggest design weakness was the $50,000 damages floor that kept most individual victims from suing directly, leaving enforcement to the FTC and state attorneys general. The five-year sunset and the securities-and-commodities carve-out were reasonable-cost compromises that an honest supporter could defend, but they weakened the protection.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed the bill by voice vote, and the Senate even agreed to the House's version with a few final changes, but the House never voted to accept those changes before the Congress ended, so the bill died without becoming law.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Bryan introduced the bill on June 26, 1991, joined by Sen. John McCain, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.
On November 27, 1991, the Commerce Committee was discharged by unanimous consent and the Senate passed the bill with an amendment by voice vote.
On September 29, 1992, the House took the bill up by unanimous consent, struck the Senate text and inserted the provisions of its similar bill H.R. 3203, and passed it without objection.
On October 7, 1992, the Senate agreed to the House version with its own final amendment by voice vote; the House never voted on that amendment before the 102nd Congress ended, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The telemarketing industry came out ahead: it never faced the FTC's rules, the calling-hour limits, or the refund requirements. Phone consumers got nothing from this Congress and would have to wait for a future Congress to pass similar protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Telemarketers — the new rules never took effect

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by a Democrat with a Republican co-introducer, and every vote in both chambers was by voice vote or unanimous consent — no member is recorded as opposing it.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed shipping deadlines, refunds, cancellation rights, calling-hour limits, recordkeeping duties, and a ban on abusive computer-generated calls on telephone sellers. Legitimate firms would bear compliance costs; fraudulent boiler rooms would lose core techniques like credit card laundering.

industries.industry: Credit card banks and card payment systems
industries.note: Banks would gain a ban on credit card laundering that lets fraudsters route charges around the card system, plus the right to sue telemarketers that cost them money. The same bill let banks delay telling customers their records had been released to authorities, which cuts against customers' privacy.
The final version exempted securities and futures professionals from FTC rules, but directed the SEC and CFTC to write similar anti-fraud telemarketing rules of their own.

The bill ordered an FTC study of unfair or deceptive practices in the life care home industry, with a report to Congress on whether to write industry-specific rules — a precursor to possible regulation rather than an immediate one.
